t.3.47.1: Having heard Sītā's words, the mighty Daśagrīva struck his hand against his hand and assumed an immense form.
t.3.47.2: Then he spoke again, vehemently, to Maithilī: "I think, mad woman, that my valour and prowess have never reached your hearing."
t.3.47.3: Standing in the sky, I could lift up the earth with my two arms; I could drink up the ocean, and standing on the battlefield I could slay Death himself.
t.3.47.4: I could obstruct the sun and split open the surface of the earth with sharp arrows. O mad woman, behold me, who can take any form at will, a husband who grants every desire!
t.3.47.6: At once casting off his gentle mendicant's guise, that Rāvaṇa, the younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa, assumed his own form, which resembled the form of Death itself.
t.3.47.5: As the enraged Rāvaṇa spoke thus, his two eyes, blazing with the radiance of fire and tawny at their corners, turned red.
t.3.47.7: The night-roaming one became ten-faced, with blood-red eyes, glorious, adorned with earrings of refined gold, bearing a bow and arrows.
t.3.47.8: Casting off that disguise of a wandering ascetic, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, huge of body, assumed his own true form.
t.3.47.9: His eyes reddened with anger, lustrous as a mass of dark rain-clouds and wearing red garments, he stood there gazing at Maithilī, that jewel among women.
t.3.47.10: Rāvaṇa spoke to her, Maithilī, whose hair-ends were black, who was like the radiance of the sun, and who was adorned with garments and ornaments.
t.3.47.11: If you desire a husband renowned throughout the three worlds, take refuge in me, O lady of beautiful hips; I am a husband worthy of you.
t.3.47.12: Be mine for a long time; I am worthy of praise and dear to you, and never anywhere, O fair lady, shall I do anything displeasing to you. Let your human attachment be abandoned, and let your affection be turned toward me.
t.3.47.13: Rāma has fallen from his kingdom, his aims are unfulfilled, and his span of life is limited; by what virtues are you devoted to him, O foolish woman who thinks herself wise?
t.3.47.14: That foolish one who, at the word of a woman, abandoned his kingdom together with his friends and kinsfolk, and now dwells in this forest roamed by beasts of prey.
t.3.47.15: Having spoken these words to Maithilī, who deserved kindness and spoke kindly, Rāvaṇa seized Sītā, as Budha in the sky seizes Rohiṇī.
t.3.47.16: With his left hand he seized the lotus-eyed Sītā by the hair, and with his right hand he grasped her by the thighs.
t.3.47.17: Seeing him, who resembled a mountain peak, sharp-fanged and mighty-armed, like Death itself, the forest deities, stricken with fear, fled away.
t.3.47.18: And then Rāvaṇa's great chariot came into view, wrought of magic, divine, yoked with asses, harsh in its sound, its body made of gold.
t.3.47.19: Then, having threatened her with harsh words, the loud-voiced one took Vaidehī up in his arms and placed her on the chariot.
t.3.47.20: Seized by Rāvaṇa, the illustrious Sītā, afflicted with grief, cried out loudly, "Rāma!", calling to Rāma, who had gone far off into the forest.
t.3.47.21: Then Rāvaṇa, tormented by desire, seized her, who did not desire him and was writhing like the wife of a serpent king, and flew up into the sky.
t.3.47.22: Then she, being carried off through the sky by the lord of the rākṣasas, cried out loudly like one intoxicated, like one afflicted, her mind bewildered.
t.3.47.23: Alas, Lakṣmaṇa, mighty-armed one, you who gladden the heart of your elder, you do not know that I am being carried off by a demon who changes form at will!
t.3.47.24: O Rāghava, you who would give up life, happiness and wealth for the sake of dharma, do you not see me being carried off through adharma?
t.3.47.25: Are you not, indeed, the chastiser of the unruly, O scorcher of foes? Why then do you not punish Rāvaṇa for such a wicked deed?
t.3.47.26: Surely the fruit of an undisciplined man's deed is not seen at once; time too plays its part here, as it does in the ripening of crops.
t.3.47.27: You have done this deed with your mind struck down by Time; now receive from Rāma a dreadful calamity that will bring an end to your life.
t.3.47.28: Alas, now Kaikeyī, together with her kinsmen, has her wish fulfilled, while this one, the lawful wife of the glorious man devoted to dharma, is carried off in shame.
t.3.47.29: I call upon Janasthāna and the blossoming karṇikāra trees: quickly tell Rāma that Rāvaṇa is carrying off Sītā!
t.3.47.30: I bow to the peaked Mālyavant and to Mount Prasravaṇa: tell Rāma quickly that Rāvaṇa is carrying off Sītā!
t.3.47.31: I salute the river Godāvarī, resounding with the cries of haṃsas and sārasas. Quickly tell Rāma that Rāvaṇa is carrying off Sītā!
t.3.47.32: And to the deities who roam in this forest of many kinds of trees, to them I bow; tell my husband that I have been carried away.
t.3.47.33: Whatever creatures dwell here, I go to them all for refuge, even to the herds of beasts and the flocks of birds.
t.3.47.35: Having learned where I am, the mighty-armed one of great strength will, by his valour, bring me back even from the other world, even were I carried off by Vaivasvata.
t.3.47.34: Of her who is being carried off, the beloved of her husband, dearer to him than his very life, proclaim this: “Sītā has been carried away helpless by Rāvaṇa.”
t.3.47.36: O Jaṭāyu, my abduction must be told to Rāma exactly as it happened, and all of it must be related to Lakṣmaṇa as well, without leaving anything out.
